p.title: Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks as An Influence Maximization Problem

ext.title: Adversarial Attack on Graph Neural Networks as an Influence Maximization Problem
ext.venue: WSDM 2022 (Fifteenth ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining), Tempe AZ, virtual, Research Paper track, pp. 675-685
ext.document_type: Conference paper (WSDM 2022 research paper, 11 pages including references and appendices)
ext.coverage: Read the full text file in chunks: lines 1-1391 and 1392-1699 (all of it), covering abstract, introduction, related work, preliminaries, Section 4 analysis (4.1-4.4, Propositions 1-2, Lemma 1, Corollaries 1-2), Section 5 experiments (Tables 1-3, Figures 2-3), conclusion, references 1-35, and Appendices A (proofs) and B (additional experiments). Metadata hint verified: title, venue, year and DOI are correct; authors confirmed from the header. Paul markup: no markup files were listed for this document, and no annotation file named d3f0c986a967.json exists in the research _annots folder (checked by filename only; the other 63 annotation files were not opened), so paul_markup is empty. Scope note: the paper has no material on lobbying, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text measurement. Network content is graph influence (linear threshold model), random-walk importance and centrality baselines.
ext.research_question: Can a restricted, realistic black-box attack on a GNN, which perturbs the features of a small set of nodes with no access to model parameters or predictions, be formalized and solved efficiently by connecting node selection to influence maximization on a threshold model? (Abstract; Sections 1 and 3.2, pp. 675-677.)
ext.theory: Adversarial attack on GNNs recast as influence maximization. Under a ReLU path-independence assumption (Assumption 1, after Xu et al. 2018), the expected mis-classification rate becomes a spread function on a directed bipartite graph with node-specific thresholds (general or linear threshold model, Kempe et al. 2003). The objective is submodular when threshold CDFs are concave on the positive domain (Proposition 2, p. 678), so greedy selection applies. Section 4.2, p. 677-678.
ext.data: Three public citation benchmarks: Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed (Sen et al. 2008; Yang et al. 2016). Unit: nodes. Graph sizes N are not stated in the text. Random 60/20/20 train/validation/test splits (Table 1 and 2); 10 percent training data in Table 3 and Appendix B.2. 40 independent trials per model-dataset pair. Victim models: GCN and GAT with 2 layers, JK-Net with 7 layers. Proxy models: 20 GCNs trained on separate splits to build the perturbation vector. Period: not stated; benchmark data only, no time period.
ext.method: Two-step attack: (1) select a node set S with |S| at most r and degree at most m; (2) add a constant perturbation vector epsilon to features of nodes in S. The paper focuses on step 1. InfMax-Unif greedily maximizes the saturated coverage objective h(S) = sum over j of (min(sum over i in S of B_ji, a) + b) divided by (a+b), with B = M^L (random-walk transition matrix, L = 4), uniform threshold distribution, a = 0.01 (Corollary 1, Eq. 6). InfMax-Norm greedily maximizes sum over j of (1 + erf(sum B_ji / (sigma sqrt 2)))/2 with sigma = 0.01 (Corollary 2, Eq. 7). Baselines: Degree, Betweenness, PageRank (alpha = 0.85), RWCS and GC-RWCS (Ma et al. 2020; L = 4, l = 30, k = 1). Constraints: r = 1 percent of graph size; m = lowest degree of the top 10 or 30 percent of nodes. Perturbation: lambda = 10, top 2 percent features by average gradient sign-consistent across 20 proxy GCNs, value in {-lambda, 0, lambda}. Significance: pairwise t-test at alpha 0.05. Section 3.2 and 5.1-5.2, pp. 676-681.
ext.identification: Not applicable in the causal sense. This is an adversarial-attack benchmark, not causal inference. Validity rests on the black-box design: proxy GCNs trained on different splits build the perturbation vector, so it does not depend on victim models. The authors note the Ma et al. 2020 setup used victim-model information (Appendix B.1).
ext.scope: Population: node-level, untargeted, evasion, black-box attacks by feature perturbation on GNNs (GCN, GAT, JK-Net) for node classification on three citation networks. Institution: University of Michigan School of Information. Era: 2022 publication on 2008-2016 public benchmarks. Excludes graph-topology perturbation and binary or nonnegative features (future work, p. 685).

key_findings.finding: The mis-classification rate objective, with model parameters replaced by their expectation, equals an influence-maximization objective on a directed bipartite graph with node thresholds theta_j (Proposition 1, Eq. 3-4).
key_findings.location: Section 4.2, Proposition 1, p. 677; proof Appendix A.1
key_findings.numbers: Influence weights B = M^L with L-step random walk; threshold theta_j = (ybar_j(empty) minus max-class logit margin) over (W_khat minus W_y)^T epsilon

key_findings.finding: Influence maximization on this bipartite linear threshold graph is NP-hard (reduction from Set Cover).
If each threshold CDF F_j is concave on [0, inf), the expected mis-classification rate h(S) is submodular in S, so greedy selection has a guarantee.
key_findings.location: Proposition 2, Section 4.3, p. 678; proof Appendix A.2

key_findings.finding: Uniform thresholds give saturated coverage objective (InfMax-Unif); normal thresholds give an erf objective (InfMax-Norm). Both are submodular.
key_findings.numbers: a = 0.01 and sigma = 0.01 fixed in all experiments; authors say results are fairly robust to these choices (p. 679)

key_findings.finding: On the 60 percent training setting, InfMax-Unif gives lower test accuracy than the strongest baseline GC-RWCS in most setups, with significance marked in Table 1. Example: Cora GAT, 10 percent threshold, 55.9 vs 57.5 (no attack 87.7). Pubmed GAT, 30 percent threshold, 64.1 vs 69.1 (no attack 85.2).
key_findings.numbers: Text says both proposed methods beat all baselines in all but 3 of 18 setups. Table 1 shows near-ties on Citeseer GCN and GAT at 10 percent (InfMax-Unif 60.7 and 62.4 vs GC-RWCS 60.5 and 62.4); the authors' count was not independently rechecked.

key_findings.finding: The 10 percent threshold setting shows Cora GCN 68.8 (InfMax-Unif) vs 70.0 (GC-RWCS), and Pubmed JK-Net 55.6 vs 56.7. Degree and Betweenness baselines are weaker than the random-walk methods.
key_findings.numbers: See Table 1 rows; Random baseline Cora JK-Net 70.5 (10 percent threshold)

key_findings.finding: Empirical threshold distributions, estimated by 1000 GCN initializations on Cora, are non-increasing on the positive domain in most cases, supporting the submodularity assumption.
key_findings.numbers: 1000 model initializations; 3 nodes shown; rho set to 1 for visualization (footnote 5)

key_findings.finding: On a stochastic blockmodel with 4 communities, the better methods (GC-RWCS and the proposed methods) spread selected nodes more evenly across communities.
With 10 percent training data and in the Ma et al. (2020) setup, the same trends hold.
key_findings.numbers: Table 3 Cora GCN no attack 81.1; InfMax-Unif 10 percent threshold 72.6 (JK-Net 58.1); the authors call the trend similar

limitations: Assumption 1 (ReLU activations independent with a common probability) is an approximation taken from Xu et al. 2018; it is a simplification of the real network.

The thresholds are treated as random. The authors say independence across nodes is unrealistic for GNNs because neighbours' predictions correlate, and they leave concentration of the mis-classification rate around its expectation to future work (Section 4.4, p. 679).
The distribution assumptions (uniform or normal thresholds) likely deviate from the real distribution; the authors state this (p. 679).
Hyperparameters a and sigma are fixed at 0.01 without tuning; the theoretically optimal choice depends on epsilon and the dataset (p. 679).
Only node selection is studied. The perturbation vector is constant across nodes (no personalization), and the attack is untargeted.
Only feature perturbation with continuous features is treated; graph-structure perturbation and binary or nonnegative features are future work (Conclusion, p. 685).
The bipartite connection uses rho (the path activation probability), which is unknown; visualization sets rho = 1 (footnote 5, p. 681).
Evaluation covers three citation benchmarks and three GNN architectures with a single attack budget r = 1 percent of graph size. Graph sizes are not reported in the text.
Greedy submodularity gives an approximation guarantee for the expected objective, not for the actual mis-classification rate. The paper does not prove the concentration of the actual rate.

measures: Test accuracy (%) after attack, with standard error over 40 independent trials (Tables 1-3).
Pairwise t-test at significance 0.05 for the difference from the best baseline.
Mis-classification rate (objective of Eq. 2) and its expectation h(S) (Eq. 5-7).
Node centralities used as baselines: degree C_D(i) = |N_i|/N; betweenness; PageRank with alpha = 0.85; random-walk column sum I(i) = sum over j of [M^L]_ji.
Threshold theta_j from logit margins (Eq. 4) and its empirical histogram over 1000 initializations (Figure 2).
Random-walk transition matrix M with L = 4 steps (B = M^L).

short_quotes.quote: the proposed attack strategies significantly degrade the performance of three popular GNN models
we follow the most strict black-box setup [19] to our knowledge, which prohibits any probing of the model
the expected mis-classification rate is submodular with respect to the selected set of nodes to perturb

rel.summary_md:
Ma, Deng and Mei (WSDM 2022) study a strict black-box attack on graph neural networks. The attacker cannot see model parameters or predictions. It may change the features of at most r nodes (1 percent of the graph), each with degree at most m. The paper's main contribution is choosing which nodes to perturb. Under a ReLU path-independence approximation, the expected misclassification rate becomes an influence-maximization objective on a directed bipartite linear-threshold graph. Influence weights are B = M^L (an L-step random walk, L = 4), and the thresholds are random. The problem is NP-hard (Lemma 1). It is submodular, so greedy selection carries a guarantee, only when each threshold CDF is concave on the positive domain (Proposition 2). Uniform thresholds give a saturated-coverage objective (InfMax-Unif) and normal thresholds give an erf objective (InfMax-Norm). On Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed, both methods usually cut test accuracy more than the GC-RWCS, PageRank, degree and betweenness baselines; degree and betweenness are the weakest. One example is Cora GAT: 87.7 with no attack, 57.5 under GC-RWCS and 55.9 under InfMax-Unif. Near-ties occur on Citeseer. A qualitative SBM case study suggests the better selectors spread their seeds across communities.

The paper does not concern legislatures, lobbying or persuasion, so nothing about political behavior transfers. What does transfer is the mathematics. Proposition 2 gives the exact condition for a greedy guarantee on a threshold model: the threshold CDF must be concave. Paul's system uses deterministic tier thresholds in lt_priming and lazy greedy over Monte Carlo spread in the frontier and coalition allocators. The paper says when those greedy claims hold and when they do not. Its other lessons are that coverage-style saturating objectives beat raw centrality, and that seed sets should avoid redundancy. The adversarial result itself has no counterpart in the system, which runs no GNN. It does give an analogy for testing how neighbour-propagated stance imputation behaves when a few node inputs are corrupted. That analogy is weak and UNVERIFIED.

bearings.paper_claim: In a general or linear threshold model with random node thresholds, the expected spread h(S) is submodular when every threshold CDF F_j is concave on [0, inf) (Proposition 2). Without that condition, linear-threshold influence maximization on the bipartite graph is NP-hard (Lemma 1, by reduction from Set Cover). Uniform thresholds give the submodular saturated-coverage objective sum_j (min(sum_i B_ji, a) + b)/(a+b) (Corollary 1, Eq. 6).
bearings.paper_location: Section 4.2-4.3, Lemma 1, Proposition 2, Corollary 1, pp. 678-679; proof Appendix A.2
bearings.system_side: lt_priming uses a linear-threshold adoption rule with DETERMINISTIC thresholds: a fixed tier ladder THETA (Highly Persuadable 0.6 up to Opponent 3.0), plus a lean term and +COMMIT per Opponent cell. Pressure is the sum of kernel probabilities from active pro neighbours. Each target is solved separately for the cheapest mix of recruits and money, and no seed-set guarantee is claimed.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the mathematics transfers; the GNN and citation-benchmark context does not. A point-mass threshold has a step CDF, which is not concave, so any future step that aggregates lt_priming targets into a seed-set objective and then cites a (1-1/e) greedy bound would be unsupported. Randomizing theta by tier (for example, uniform around the ladder value) would make the bound available, at the cost of an unestimated spread parameter. The per-target cheapest-tip solve is unaffected. Moderate for the mathematical condition, weak for empirical relevance.

bearings.paper_claim: Selectors that account for overlap in coverage (InfMax-Unif and InfMax-Norm through saturation, and GC-RWCS) beat selectors that rank nodes by stand-alone importance (degree, betweenness, PageRank). In Table 1 the proposed methods beat all baselines in all but 3 of 18 setups (authors' count); for example, Pubmed GAT at the 30% threshold gives 64.1 vs 69.1 for GC-RWCS (85.2 with no attack). In an SBM with 4 communities, the better selectors spread seeds more evenly across communities (Figure 3, qualitative, no statistic).
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.2 Table 1, pp. 680-681; Section 5.4 Figure 3, p. 681
bearings.system_side: The coalition allocator ranks the top-45 neutral candidates by SINGLETON marginal spread({n}) - base. It boosts that by (1 + 0.8 bpf) and water-fills $2M in proportion. Redundancy among funded seeds enters only through the joint spread reported afterwards; it never shapes the selection.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's objective is GNN misclassification on citation graphs at a 1% node budget. The CU objective is a Monte Carlo competitive cascade on the cosponsor kernel. The transferable point is structural: ranking by singleton marginals ignores overlap, so funded seeds can cluster in one community. The code already measures the joint-vs-naive gap ('naive-additive'). Comparing the singleton-marginal set against a lazy-greedy set (budget_frontier already implements one) would show whether the gap matters. The paper's community-spread finding is qualitative. Weak to moderate.

bearings.paper_claim: A saturated, coverage-style objective over L-step random-walk influence B = M^L (L = 4) is submodular and outperforms one-step and centrality heuristics. Influence is counted over multi-hop walks with a cap per receiver (a = 0.01), not over direct ties.
bearings.paper_location: Corollary 1 Eq. 6, Section 4.3, p. 678-679; Section 5.1 settings, p. 679
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit performs cost-bounded max-coverage greedy with cov[v] = 1 - prod(1 - p) over the selected recruiters' DIRECT edge probabilities. It claims (1-1/e) through monotone submodular coverage, with GCOMB-style locality and degree pruning. Coverage is one hop.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports a saturating coverage surrogate as a well-founded submodular stand-in for threshold spread, and it independently backs the existing (1-1/e) claim for this mode. The extension is multi-hop coverage: replace p with an L-step walk-weighted reach on the kernel. On the cosponsor graph, M would be the degree-normalized kernel, so the result is a heuristic reach score (D-025), not an introduction probability. It must not become per-edge volume normalization, which was REJECTED. Weak.

bearings.paper_claim: As seed selectors, plain centralities are weaker than random-walk column sums with saturation. In Table 1, Degree and Betweenness fall below RWCS, GC-RWCS and InfMax, and PageRank (alpha 0.85) is intermediate. Random-walk column sum I(i) = sum_j [M^L]_ji is the importance measure behind the strongest baseline.
bearings.paper_location: Section 5.1 baselines and Section 5.2 Table 1, pp. 679-681
bearings.system_side: kb_benchmark computes Katz-Bonacich centrality, b = (I - dA)^-1 1 with delta = 0.85/lambda_max, on the live kernel P = build_P(adj). It counts weighted out-walks, and is used only as a Spearman diagnostic against allocations, money and the legislative score; the chain never consumes it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Katz-Bonacich is a walk-sum importance measure close to RWCS (unnormalized and infinite-horizon rather than L = 4). The paper's evidence that unsaturated walk sums leave value on the table, relative to coverage-aware selection, fits the system's choice to keep KB diagnostic only. The paper concerns attack selection on GNN benchmarks, not legislators, so this is context only, and KB scores remain heuristic outputs (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Perturbing the features of only 1% of nodes, chosen by an influence-maximization criterion, sharply lowers the accuracy of graph-propagating predictors (GCN, GAT, JK-Net). An example is Cora GAT, which falls from 87.7 to 55.9 at the 10% degree threshold. Propagation through the graph is what lets a few nodes affect many predictions.
bearings.system_side: Neighbour imputation proposes a tier for a silent (member, issue) cell from the mean TSCORE of at least 5 labelled cosponsor neighbours, kept when |est| >= 0.75. Masking validation reports about 77% sign agreement. These are proposals only; the matrix is unchanged.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The system has no GNN. It uses a one-hop mean and a human-adjudicated output, so propagation is shallow and an adversary is implausible. The transferable idea is a robustness check: perturb or flip the labels of a few high-coverage members, chosen by walk-coverage rather than at random, and measure how many proposals change sign. That would separate label-error sensitivity from the 77% agreement figure. Weak; any result is UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062).

gaps_exposed: No greedy step states whether its objective is submodular. budget_frontier and per_topic_coalition run lazy greedy or marginal ranking over a competitive cascade with bystander activation. The paper shows that a guarantee needs a specific structural condition (concave threshold CDF), so a (1-1/e) bound should not be assumed from greedy alone.
lt_priming's thresholds are deterministic tier constants. A seed-set version of LT priming would have no greedy guarantee, and NP-hardness applies (Lemma 1).

The coalition allocator funds by singleton marginals and checks redundancy only afterwards (joint vs naive-additive). There is no overlap-aware selection like that of the coverage-objective methods, which beat stand-alone-importance baselines.
There is no robustness test of graph-propagated estimates (neighbour imputation, cascade spreads) against a few corrupted or mislabelled high-coverage nodes.
Coverage in budgetRecruit is one hop. Multi-hop, saturating reach has not been tried.
flags: The paper's 'influence' means spread of misclassification in a GNN. It is not legislator influence, and its results must not be quoted as evidence about persuasion, lobbying or access.
Random-walk importance B = M^L and walk-sum centralities are heuristic model outputs, never closeness, access or introduction probabilities (D-025).

Porting M = D^-1 A to the cosponsor graph normalizes by node degree. Check that it does not bring back the REJECTED per-edge volume-normalization proposal under another name. The paper itself argues for neither rejected SNA proposal.
Table 1 figures come from 3 citation benchmarks, 40 trials and a 1% node budget, with no graph sizes reported. Any number quoted must carry that window and denominator.
The paper's count of 'all but 3 of 18 setups' was not independently rechecked, and Citeseer at the 10% threshold shows near-ties.
rel.paul_alignment: The paper sharpens Paul's own caution. His margin note on Chen 2023 says pressure from high-ranking members is "not diminishing", which he reads as a challenge to submodular assumptions. Proposition 2 makes that exact: the greedy guarantee holds only when the threshold CDF is concave. Non-diminishing or step-like threshold responses break it. Paul's three-tier architecture places the per-topic allocators in a "static and submodular" tier. As built, those allocators run greedy over a competitive cascade with bystander mobilization, and the code never establishes submodularity. Labelling that tier submodular is therefore an assumption, not a property. His GCOMB and CELF expectations for the joint optimizer are untouched, because that optimizer is separable and concave per member. Paul has no annotation on this paper.

related.why: Complex contagion is the non-concave-threshold case where Proposition 2's submodularity fails. The two papers together bound when greedy seeding is justified.
Competitive LT models can lose submodularity, which the flip model already cites. Ma et al. give the single-campaign condition (concave CDF) under which it is recovered.
Both rely on the submodularity-implies-greedy-guarantee result. Ma et al. derive submodularity from the threshold distribution, the property Golovin and Krause assume.

Almazaydeh argues centrality heuristics rival greedy in influence maximization. Ma et al. find degree, betweenness and PageRank weaker than greedy on a coverage objective, though in a GNN-attack setting.
Both connect GNNs and influence maximization in opposite directions: Kumar uses GNNs to solve influence maximization, and Ma et al. use influence maximization to attack GNNs.
If a temporal GNN stance model is adopted, the restricted black-box node-perturbation vulnerability shown here becomes a direct robustness concern.
